User wants help balancing a training calendar for soccer, cycling, yoga, triathlon, and now 10K running.

General availability/preferences:
- Weekdays: 7:00–9:00 am
- Weekends: 8:00 am–12:00 pm
- Yoga: 2×/week, 45 min
- Cycling: 1×/week, 2 hr
- Soccer: 1×/week, 1.5 hr
- Triathlon: 3×/week, varying durations
- Prioritize triathlon training on weekends
- Wants 1 rest day/week
- Sprint triathlon goal: June 24 (year unspecified)
- Fitness: intermediate yoga/cycling, beginner swimming, advanced running
- Latest reported charity 5K PB: 26:30 (overwrite earlier 27:45 figure; if dates/context matter, clarify which is accurate)

A prior triathlon sample schedule:
- Mon 7:00–7:45 yoga
- Tue 7:00–9:00 triathlon brick (30 min each swim/cycle/run)
- Wed 7:00–8:30 triathlon cycling
- Thu 7:00–7:45 yoga
- Fri 7:00–8:30 soccer
- Sat 8:00–9:00 triathlon swim, 10:00–12:00 cycling
- Sun 8:00–10:00 triathlon run/brick
- This contains no actual rest day and is overloaded. If revising, include exactly one genuine rest day, avoid stacking too many sessions, and clearly label any combined sessions.

Saturday group ride:
- Wants a 20-mile moderate group route
- Prefers rolling terrain with a few short steeper hills
- Wants quieter secondary roads, scenic views, and bike-friendly infrastructure
- Should start/end at the same local park used for the charity 5K
- User says they are in “Oakdale,” want to avoid downtown and highways, and know the river bike trail
- Critical ambiguity: Oakdale exists in multiple states, and the park/river-trail starting point was never identified. Previously suggested Oakdale Marina, Oakbrook Drive, Maple Street, Elm Avenue, Parkview Drive, Highland Avenue, and River Road were unverified placeholders/inventions, not a real route. Obtain state/country, precise park or map pin, desired trail access, and waypoints before proposing actual roads.
- Useful tools: Strava Route Builder, Ride with GPS, MapMyRide, Google Maps cycling mode.
- Do not invent cafe stops; verify business, location, hours, and bike access.

10K running:
- Event is in about 12 weeks
- Goal: finish under 55 minutes
- Current routine: 3 runs/week—one weekend long run and two shorter weekday runs
- Average pace: ~9:30/mile
- Prefers morning running and is available any day
- No reported injuries
- Comfortable with speed work and hill repeats
- Recently requested a more aggressive plan based on the 5K PB

Prior 12-week plan structure:
- Weeks 1–4 base: 3 runs/week; long run 6–7 miles, two short runs 3–4 miles, plus one strength session
- Weeks 5–6 speed: 6–8×800 m, suggested around 8:15–8:30/mile, with 400 m active recovery; easy warmup/cooldown; weekend long run
- Weeks 7–8 hills: 6–8×400 m hill repeats with 200 m active recovery; easy run
- Weeks 9–10 pace: 3–4 miles around 8:30–8:45/mile; easy run
- Weeks 11–12 taper: reduce volume 20–30% and retain easy runs
- Prior plan sets ordinary “easy” runs around 8:45–9:15/mile and long runs around 9:00–9:15/mile; these may be too aggressive for many runners and should generally be conversational, not fixed near threshold.
- Do not infer lactate-threshold pace directly or confidently from a 5K time. A 26:30 5K may suggest a sub-55 10K is plausible under favorable conditions, but terrain, weather, durability, race preparation, and current training matter. Reassess after a timed 5–10K or threshold workout.
- Aggressive fixed paces/repetitions should not be prescribed before checking recent race effort, threshold pace, weekly mileage, recovery, and symptoms. Favor one hard workout plus easy running, avoid back-to-back hard days, retain rest, and recommend medical evaluation for pain or altered gait.
- Need reconcile the 10K plan with the triathlon/soccer/yoga/cycling schedule rather than treating running as an isolated plan.

Bike computer/GPS shopping:
- User previously asked for options to track rides.
- Earlier suggestions included Garmin Edge 130, Wahoo ELEMNT, Lezyne Super GPS, and watches such as Garmin Forerunner 945, Polar Vantage V, and Suunto 3 Fitness.
- Some descriptions were inaccurate: most dedicated bike computers lack built-in heart-rate sensing unless explicitly stated; they generally require external sensors. Forerunner 945 is a watch, not a bike computer.
- Future comparisons should ask about budget, maps/navigation, phone-free use, route guidance, HR/power/cadence support, battery, display, apps/ecosystem, and mounting; verify current models, prices, and features.

User prefers practical, shareable, group-friendly plans. Recommendations should be safety-conscious, realistic, and fact-checked.
